ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Neuro-Oncology Consultation — Wilma Rudolph

code.originalText: MRI result: left frontal mass with edema; dexamethasone, CT staging, neuro-oncology consultation with neurosurgery, and preparation for awake craniotomy

text.paragraph: Three weeks of headaches on waking, with ten days of word-finding pauses and clumsiness of the right hand, in a previously well 54-year-old hospital executive and former Olympic sprinter. Examination today shows mild expressive language difficulty, a slight right pronator drift and right grip weakness. MRI of the brain with and without contrast is booked for tomorrow morning. Please see her within a week, with neurosurgery, to review the MRI with her and plan diagnosis and treatment if it shows a tumor. [S]
Urgency: Within one week; the same day if the MRI shows a mass with shift or she worsens. [S]

list.item: What does the MRI show, what is the most likely diagnosis, and is any further imaging needed before surgery?
Do you recommend biopsy or resection, and how can her language and right-hand function be protected?
Which pathology and molecular tests are needed for the diagnosis?
If this is a high-grade glioma, what treatment should follow surgery?
How should steroids, seizures and the risk of blood clots be managed, and what should primary care monitor?

text.paragraph: Ms. Rudolph, 54, is seen with the neurosurgery team at the request of Dr. Haynes-Whitaker, three days after she reported three weeks of morning headaches and ten days of word-finding pauses and right-hand clumsiness. The MRI the next morning showed a left frontal mass, and dexamethasone 4 mg twice a day was started that afternoon; since then her headache has eased and her speech has improved. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis yesterday showed no cancer elsewhere. She has had no seizure. She had polio as a small child, which left her left leg paralyzed for some years; she recovered fully and became an Olympic sprinter. She works as a hospital vice president, is right-handed, and wants the facts given plainly. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Wilma Glodean Rudolph was born on June 23, 1940, in Saint Bethlehem, Tennessee, near Clarksville, the twentieth of twenty-two children in her father's family. She grew up in a large, poor Black family in the segregated South. [D]
She was born prematurely and weighed about 4.5 pounds at birth. [D]
She was often ill as a small child: at about age four she had double pneumonia followed by scarlet fever, and she had a number of other childhood illnesses before polio. [D]
In early childhood she had polio, which left her left leg paralyzed or partly paralyzed, with the foot turned inward. Sources give her age at the illness as an infant, about four, or about five. [D]

She wore a metal leg brace for several years (from about age six to ten in one account) and a specially made shoe. Once a week her mother took her by bus to Nashville, a 90-minute round trip, to the closest doctors who would treat her in the segregated South: physicians at Meharry Medical College, a historically Black medical school, fitted the brace and prescribed massage and heat. At home her family massaged the leg several times a day. [D]

She later wrote that a doctor told her she would never walk again, and that her mother told her she would. Accounts of her recovery differ: she took the brace off in public at about nine and a half, could move about with the brace by eight, was running by eleven, and no longer needed the brace by about twelve. [D]

At sixteen she won a bronze medal in the 4 x 100-meter relay at the 1956 Olympic Games in Melbourne. At the 1960 Games in Rome she won gold in the 100 meters, the 200 meters and the 4 x 100-meter relay, the first American woman to win three gold medals in track and field at one Olympics. She ran for the Tennessee State University Tigerbelles. [D]

After retiring from competition she worked in teaching, coaching and community work, founded an organization to help amateur track and field athletes, and in 1992 returned to Tennessee as a vice president of a Nashville hospital. [D]

list.item: Left posterior frontal ring-enhancing mass, presumed high-grade glioma (D49.6). A single necrotic ring-enhancing mass with raised perfusion in a woman of 54 without cancer elsewhere on CT is most likely a glioblastoma. A solitary metastasis has been made unlikely by the CT; lymphoma would usually enhance solidly and restrict diffusion; an abscess would restrict diffusion in its center. The mass sits just behind the expressive language area and in front of the motor strip, and the edema explains much of her symptoms. Maximal safe resection, rather than biopsy alone, gives the tissue diagnosis, relieves the mass effect and improves survival, and an awake craniotomy with cortical and subcortical language and motor mapping lets the surgeons remove the tumor while protecting speech and hand function. A functional MRI with tractography beforehand will show the language areas and the motor tract. The tissue needs an integrated WHO CNS5 diagnosis: IDH1 R132H immunostaining, with IDH1 and IDH2 sequencing if it is negative because she is 54, ATRX and p53, the TERT promoter, EGFR amplification and chromosome 7 gain with 10 loss, which define glioblastoma when IDH is wild-type, CDKN2A, histone H3 and BRAF, and MGMT promoter methylation, which predicts benefit from temozolomide. If this is a glioblastoma, the standard after surgery is radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with daily temozolomide 75 mg/m2, Pneumocystis prophylaxis and weekly blood counts, then six cycles of adjuvant temozolomide, with tumor-treating fields offered for the adjuvant phase, and screening for a clinical trial. Dexamethasone is right for edema causing symptoms and should be tapered as soon as possible after surgery. She has had no seizure, so she should not have a prophylactic antiseizure drug. Brain tumors carry a high risk of venous thromboembolism: she needs mechanical and then heparin prophylaxis in hospital after surgery, but not routinely at home. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Haynes-Whitaker's intake note. MRI of the brain with and without contrast, with diffusion and perfusion: a 3.8 x 3.2 cm ring-enhancing mass in the left posterior frontal lobe involving the posterior inferior frontal gyrus and abutting the precentral gyrus, with central necrosis, raised relative cerebral blood volume in the rim, no restricted diffusion in the necrotic center, surrounding edema and 5 mm midline shift; no other lesion. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis: no primary tumor or other lesion. Today: hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, white cells 11.8 on dexamethasone, platelets 270; sodium 140, potassium 4.0, creatinine 0.84 mg/dL; glucose 138 mg/dL not fasting; INR 1.0, aPTT 29 seconds. [S]

list.item: Functional MRI with diffusion tensor tractography in four days. [S]
Awake left frontal craniotomy with language and motor mapping for maximal safe resection in six days, with an MRI within 48 hours of surgery. [S]

Integrated WHO CNS5 diagnosis: IDH1 R132H immunostaining with IDH1 and IDH2 sequencing if negative, ATRX, p53, TERT promoter, EGFR, chromosome 7 and 10, CDKN2A, histone H3, BRAF and MGMT promoter methylation. [S]

If glioblastoma: radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with temozolomide 75 mg/m2 daily, then six cycles of temozolomide 150 to 200 mg/m2 on days 1 to 5 every 28 days; Pneumocystis prophylaxis during concurrent treatment and while lymphopenia lasts; antiemetic before each dose; tumor-treating fields offered with adjuvant temozolomide; clinical trial screening. [S]
Dexamethasone 4 mg twice a day with famotidine until surgery, then a taper to stop within a few weeks; glucose checks while on the steroid. [S]
No prophylactic antiseizure drug; levetiracetam if a seizure occurs; seizure first aid for her household. [S]
Mechanical and then low-molecular-weight heparin prophylaxis in hospital after surgery; no routine prophylaxis at home; teach the signs of leg clot and pulmonary embolism. [S]

For primary care: weekly blood counts during chemoradiation and on day 22 of each adjuvant cycle, liver tests at baseline and before each cycle, MRI four weeks after radiotherapy and then every two to three months read with allowance for pseudoprogression, physical therapy and fall prevention given her new right-sided weakness and old left-leg polio, no driving for now, distress screening, and an early palliative care referral. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Haynes-Whitaker, who saw her the same day. The MRI and the plan were explained to Ms. Rudolph with the images, and she agreed to the awake craniotomy; she decides who else receives this note. [S]
Follow-up: Surgery in six days; review with the integrated diagnosis and the tumor board recommendation before radiotherapy; Dr. Haynes-Whitaker continues primary care and shares the monitoring. [S]
